# `( )` — Group / Rows / Train

Parentheses round an expression group it, whatever it holds. Without `⋄`, they hold one expression wherever they appear, including inside [brackets](brackets.qmd). Put a literal argument after a literal operand in parentheses, as in `f⍣2(3)`. Without parentheses, `f⍣2 3` takes `2 3` as the operand.

```bpl
(2×3)+4            ⍝ 10
x←2 4 9
[(+/x) ≢x]         ⍝ 15 3ₓ
1+⍣3(5)            ⍝ 8
```

Parentheses group a glyph or a name as they group a literal: `(1 2)` is `1 2`, `(x)` is `x`, and `(-)` is `-`. For a scalar, use [`⊂`](enclose.qmd) on a subject, as in `⊂[1 2]`, or [`ᵘ`](superscript.qmd) on a function, as in `+ᵘ`.

```bpl
(5)≡5              ⍝ $t
⍴(1 2)             ⍝ [2]ₓ
x←1 2 ⋄ (x)≡x      ⍝ $t
(-)3               ⍝ ¯3
f←- ⋄ (f)3         ⍝ ¯3
```

A line break inside parentheses counts as a space. Outside brackets, spaces separate runs. Each run is grouped as if it were in parentheses. This expression means `(1+2)×(3+4)`:

```bpl
total←(1+2
       × 3+4)
total              ⍝ 21
```

## Rows

Parentheses with `⋄` are used to write a vector whose items are the rows. Each row is a vector, even a row with one item. Rows can differ in length. With a trailing `⋄`, the result is a one-item vector holding one row. Rows written over several lines need `⋄` at the end of each line.

```bpl
(4 ⋄ 4 5 ⋄ 4 5 6)       ⍝ [[4] [4 5] [4 5 6]]
a←1 ⋄ b←2
(a b ⋄ b)               ⍝ [[1 2] [2]]
(1 2 ⋄)                 ⍝ [[1 2]]
```

In brackets, rows separated by `⋄` form one array instead: `[1 2 ⋄ 3 4]` is a matrix, and `(1 2 ⋄ 3 4)` is a vector of two vectors. Write a vector of strings or of names in brackets: `["ab" "cd"]` or `[a b]`.

## Trains

Two functions form an atop: `(f g)Y` is `f(g Y)`.

```bpl
(- +/)1 2 3        ⍝ ¯6
(-×)3              ⍝ ¯1ₓ
```

Three form a fork: `(f g h)Y` is `(f Y)g(h Y)`. Dyadic forks pass both arguments to each arm.

```bpl
(+/÷≢)2 4 9        ⍝ 5
(+/ ÷ ≢)2 4 9      ⍝ 5
```

Longer trains group from the right. A fork's left arm can be a subject. The right arm evaluates first.
